units.title: The digital age: Are we ready?
units.title_zh: 数字时代：我们准备好了吗？

section_a.question: What problem led the club to run a listening experiment?
options: The library had banned all electronic devices.
Students wanted to replace every class with a club meeting.
Members felt disconnected despite frequent digital contact.
The group needed to test a new messaging application.
section_a.explanation: The club noticed that being constantly connected did not always help people feel heard.

section_a.question: What changed by the third listening session?
options: Pauses became useful, and listeners chose their words more carefully.
Participants stopped using online tools for planning.
Every participant agreed that phones should be banned.
The club replaced discussion with written reports.
section_a.explanation: The second world describes how participants grew more comfortable with pauses and attentive listening.

section_a.question: What limitation did the organizers place on their notes?
options: They were collected before the activity began.
They measured the quality of the students' devices.
They proved that online friendships were harmful.
They described one club's experience, not a rule for everyone.
section_a.explanation: The passage explicitly distinguishes local observations from universal scientific proof.

section_a.question: According to the final world, what does digital readiness involve?
options: Answering every notification as quickly as possible

Avoiding conversation whenever a device is available
Using the same communication routine in every situation
section_a.explanation: Readiness is framed as intentional choice: use a tool when it serves the need, and make room for conversation when it matters.

options: It guarantees that every viewpoint appears equally often.
It decides when a student should sleep.
It removes the need to make privacy choices.
It filters posts and may repeatedly surface selected stories.
section_b.explanation: The opening world explains that algorithms filter feeds, so repeated exposure should not be mistaken for a balanced view.

options: To avoid communicating with classmates altogether
To make it easier to return attention to the study task
To make every virtual meeting longer
To remove all notifications from their devices
section_b.explanation: The class found that opening a device between tasks made it harder to resume the original question.

section_b.question: What did the cyber safety instructor ask students to consider?
options: Whether a link, request, or post has consequences before they act
Whether all public posts should be deleted
How to avoid using a platform for school work
Why a privacy setting makes every online choice safe
section_b.explanation: The instructor teaches deliberate choices about links, password requests, and public posts.

section_b.question: Which practice helped students restore balance?
options: Checking each message as soon as it arrives
Joining several virtual groups at once
Keeping a device-free meal and a clear end time for study
Treating every long evening online as an addiction
section_b.explanation: Small planned routines, including offline time, helped protect attention, rest, and interaction.

section_c.question: What was the local health center trying to make easier?
options: Replacing all local staff with a remote application
Moving older residents to the coastal city
Making routine specialist advice available without an unnecessary long trip
Collecting health information for public social media
section_c.explanation: The first world introduces a local service designed to reduce avoidable travel for routine advice.

options: The local clinicians
The patient's distant family members alone
The makers of the telemedicine device

section_c.explanation: Remote doctors reviewed information, while local clinicians stayed responsible for follow-up.

options: It works only when every patient owns the same phone.
It removes the need to protect private information.
It makes local health professionals unnecessary.
It cannot replace every examination or suit every village.
section_c.explanation: The third world warns that online advice is not a universal substitute for in-person examination.

section_c.question: How does the final world define meaningful digital progress?
options: By the number of screens installed in a community
By whether residents can participate safely and with dignity
By how quickly a remote platform can process every request
By replacing community services with one central system
section_c.explanation: The conclusion measures progress by safe, dignified participation and shared responsibility, not by devices alone.

section_a.title: Connection or conversation
section_a.passage: A campus conversation club met each Thursday in a room that looked out over the library courtyard. Its members could send a message in seconds, yet during shared breaks some sat together without knowing how to begin. Several said they felt lonely even while their screens filled with names, photos, and alerts. The club asked a practical question: what kind of connection does this moment need? To explore it, student organizers designed a four-week listening experiment for learning, not a scientific study. At each session, members placed their devices in a basket for twenty minutes and took turns describing a small challenge. The listener had to ask one follow-up question and summarize what they had heard before replying. The rule felt awkward at first, and some participants were anxious that an urgent message might arrive. By the third session, a pause no longer seemed like a failure; it gave people time to choose words carefully. Members began noticing tone, hesitation, and the meaning behind a brief answer. They did not stop using group chats or video calls, which remained useful for planning and maintaining distant friendships. A quick digital message worked well when information was simple and time was short. A face-to-face conversation offered something different: people could revise an idea, respond to emotion, and build trust. The club's notes described its own practice, not proof that every student needed the same routine. That limit made the experiment more useful, because it invited discussion instead of imposing a universal rule. Readiness for the digital age therefore means choosing a tool with a purpose, rather than treating every notification as a command. On busy days, members used a shared calendar to protect an uninterrupted study session. On difficult days, they put phones away and asked a friend to listen before giving advice. Their goal was not less technology, but more intentional communication and a clearer sense of when to converse. Each Thursday ended with one question: did today's connection help someone feel understood?

section_b.title: Living in the digital world
section_b.passage: For many students, the digital world begins before breakfast, when a notification lights up a device beside the bed. A student may intend to check one message and then scroll through a platform for several minutes. An algorithm filters the feed, quietly deciding which stories appear again and which disappear. Because the stream feels personal, users can mistake repeated exposure for a balanced view of the world. That is why digital literacy starts with attention: notice what a platform asks you to do, and decide whether it deserves the next minute. A first-year class tested a simple habit plan for two weeks, keeping short notes on when they checked screens during study. They found that opening a device between tasks often made it harder to return to the original question. Trying to multitask did not remove the work; it scattered the attention needed to understand complex ideas. The students began grouping messages into set check-in times and placing one offline study block on their daily schedule. One student found virtual study groups useful, provided that members agreed on a goal before joining. Another reviewed privacy settings after learning how much information a default profile could reveal. A cyber safety instructor asked the class to treat each link, password request, and public post as a choice with consequences. The lesson was not to fear every platform but to understand how its tools filter information and shape habits. When a data leak or unwanted contact occurs, prevention is valuable; afterwards, calm reporting and account changes matter too. Students also discussed screen addiction without using the term as a casual label for every long evening online. A habit becomes concerning when it repeatedly harms sleep, learning, or relationships and a person cannot easily adjust it. Restored balance came from small changes: a mindful walk between lectures, a device-free meal, and a clear end time for study. During an offline hour, roommates noticed more interaction and solved small disagreements before they grew. These routines did not make the internet less powerful; they helped students use it more deliberately. Living well online is not a contest to stay disconnected, but a practice of protecting attention, privacy, and human presence.

section_c.title: Stories of China
section_c.passage: This original practice story is set in a fictional mountain county, where the nearest specialist clinic is several hours from some villages. A local health center wanted older residents to receive advice without turning every checkup into a long journey. It partnered with doctors in a coastal teaching hospital and used a secure telemedicine platform to review basic scans. The small team added a familiar phone and a private room so patients could ask questions with a nurse nearby. At first, the technology was only one part of a bigger plan. Local staff helped residents learn how to place the device, describe symptoms, and ask for a second explanation. When a connection failed, the center recorded questions and arranged a call-back instead of pretending the screen had solved everything. Doctors reviewed images carefully and sent written guidance to local clinicians, who remained responsible for follow-up care. A daughter living far away could join one appointment, but the patient still chose what information to share. The process respected privacy as well as distance. This fictional example does not claim that every village has the same service or that online advice can replace an examination. It shows why human communication matters when a new tool enters healthcare. The clinic kept an offline option for people who lacked a suitable phone, steady signal, or confidence using an app. Volunteers explained how the service worked, while medical staff checked whether the advice was clear and useful. Gradually, families spent less time arranging travel for routine questions and more time planning care with local professionals. The change depended on trust, accessible design, and patient choice rather than on a device alone. Stories of China can include this kind of practical innovation: people using knowledge and technology to solve a local need. Its value is measured not by how advanced a screen looks, but by whether residents can participate safely. A shared project becomes stronger when city doctors, county clinicians, families, and public services each take a clear role. In that sense, digital progress is a human achievement: it expands connection while keeping dignity, responsibility, and community in view.

listening.title: Listening: The digital age: Are we ready?
listening.script: In our first-year seminar, we kept a seven-day attention diary. I expected it to be a list of screen hours, but the useful question was what I had meant to do each time I picked up my device. On Monday, I opened a message during a reading task and followed a platform recommendation into several unrelated posts. The algorithm had not forced me to stay; it had made the next item easy to see. My group designed a small plan. We set two message check-in times, left urgent calls available, and used a twenty-five-minute offline block for reading. A classmate also showed us how to review privacy settings and check a link before entering account details. The plan did not remove virtual meetings or online research. It helped us choose them with a purpose. By Friday, I was still using the same phone, but I had fewer accidental interruptions and more time to finish one task before starting another. We learned that balance is not a perfect number of online and offline minutes. It is the ability to notice a habit, protect attention, and make room for real interaction when a conversation matters.

section_a.title: Two Lives, One Lesson
section_a.passage: The class opened an exhibit called Lives in Motion in the campus archive, where biographies were read as sequences of choices. Its task was not to rank remarkable people, but to ask which evidence could explain a turning point. One case followed Zheng He, the explorer whose fleet traveled across Indian Ocean routes in the early fifteenth century. Another introduced Audrey Hepburn, whose public portrait later became linked to a humanitarian mission for children. Though the lives belonged to different eras and different professions, students searched for a shared question: what does service require? The first group placed maps and port names beside a short narrative of the voyage. Records show that trade goods moved across sea routes, yet a map cannot tell every story of the people along them. Students marked documented details in blue and their own interpretations in amber. This color code helped them witness the difference between a source and a conclusion. It also kept the display from presenting one simple motive as the whole explanation. In the second case, the class examined why an ambitious performer might use fame to draw attention to children's needs. They learned that Hepburn served UNICEF as Goodwill Ambassador and traveled to Ethiopia in 1988 to highlight the drought's effects. Her work did not mean one visitor could solve a complex crisis. It showed how compassion and sustained attention could support a wider humanitarian effort. Students compared what the sources stated with what a reader might only infer. When they turned to the final wall, neither figure seemed like a ready-made model for every life. The students could admire particular choices without treating a famous person as perfect. They described a legacy as influence people inherit, question, and sometimes continue in new ways. The exhibit's narrative joined evidence, context, and consequences instead of relying on a dramatic portrait. Each visitor left with one question about ambition, responsibility, and the next action they could take.

section_b.title: Audrey Hepburn — a real angel in the world
section_b.passage: Students built an original exhibit about Audrey Hepburn, and they started with the familiar elegant portrait on a screen. The image opened a door, but it could not tell visitors everything about a life. A biography becomes richer when it places public work beside career and context. Their teacher asked them to separate documented events from assumptions about a famous person's private thoughts. That rule turned the display into a lesson in evidence, not a shrine. The class added one verified fact: Hepburn served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. In 1988 she traveled to Ethiopia to raise awareness of drought affecting children and women. Her mission brought a humanitarian concern into view, but did not claim that one person could end a crisis. Students explained why a public witness can help an audience notice a problem. They also asked whose experience should be heard first: the people living with that problem. A local organization may understand needs that an outsider cannot see from a brief visit. For that reason, charity work needs listening, accountability, and long-term partnership as well as attention. Compassion is not a decoration added to a portrait; it is a reason to respond thoughtfully. Supporting a humanitarian mission also requires perseverance, because public attention alone cannot sustain long-term work. They admired her devotion without claiming that fame guarantees wisdom. The discussion made one tension visible: publicity can open a door, yet it can also simplify people's lives. Students revised their headline to include both career and service. A second panel told how readers can check dates and original sources before repeating a claim. Instead of copying a dramatic quotation, they wrote a precise summary and named the source. The exhibit closed by asking visitors to find one responsible action that could inspire others in their community.

section_c.title: Stories of China
section_c.passage: The class opened a chart room to study Zheng He's voyages as a historical narrative rather than a legend. Their guide explained that historians describe seven expeditions across the Indian Ocean in the early fifteenth century. The students began with a fleet route and traced the names of ports recorded in maps and written accounts. The archive showed that the voyages carried goods including silk, porcelain, medicines, and metal objects to trading ports. A route map helped them imagine distance, but also reminded them that maps select what to show. The group labeled locations and directions before drawing any conclusion about the purpose of a stop. Each stop was discussed as a place where people met, exchanged goods, and made decisions. Trade is one documented purpose, and historical records can reveal how maritime networks connected regions. However, no single map can witness every conversation or explain every participant's experience. The learners compared a chart with written descriptions rather than treating either source as complete. This practice made the lesson more remarkable than memorizing a list of destinations. One student asked whether a modern reader should admire a voyage without asking difficult questions. The class agreed that respect for achievement and careful criticism can exist together. They separated evidence about routes from broader claims about what every encounter meant. That distinction kept the story open to more than one question. A voyage can reveal planning, navigation, and exchange, while still leaving gaps in the record. The fleet's legacy is therefore a useful subject for comparing past and present ideas of connection. The class placed a route-map model beside a note about how historical knowledge is built. The display invited visitors to follow an explorer's path, then inspect the sources that support the narrative. At the exit, each learner wrote one question inspired by the map and one fact they could verify.

listening.title: Listening: Life stories
listening.script: In our seminar, we compared two biographies from different eras. One account described an explorer and the fleet that traveled across the Indian Ocean; another followed Audrey Hepburn from a celebrated film career to humanitarian work. Our instructor gave us a simple rule: write down what a source shows, then mark what is still an interpretation. A map helped us trace a voyage and identify ports, but it could not witness every conversation along the route. A public portrait showed an elegant image, but it could not explain a whole mission. We learned that Hepburn served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador and traveled to Ethiopia in 1988 to raise awareness of drought affecting children and women. That fact helped us discuss how a public figure may draw attention to a need without replacing local knowledge or long-term work. One student asked whether admiration meant we should stop questioning a biography. Our mentor said the opposite: careful questions make respect more thoughtful. We compared records, checked dates, and revised a sentence that had gone beyond its evidence. The lesson was not to choose one remarkable life as a model for everyone. It was to notice ambition, perseverance, and compassion, then ask what action fits our own community. Stories can inspire us when we read them with curiosity and care.

section_a.title: The Surprising Purpose of Travel
section_a.passage: Many students imagine a successful trip as reaching a famous destination, taking clear photos, and returning without delay. Their itinerary lists landmarks in order, while a light bag of luggage keeps every step efficient. A campus travel seminar asked whether this plan explains what a journey can change. Its learners compared three journals rather than treating one traveler as a model for everyone. They found that travel also depends on curiosity: noticing details that a hurried schedule might hide. One journal belonged to a solo traveler whose train connection was cancelled before departure. Instead of calling the day a failure, she used a map to navigate a nearby neighborhood. She chose a quieter route, asked a local bookshop owner for directions, and began to wander. That brief encounter led to a conversation about the river, old streets, and everyday work. The new landscape became memorable not because it was famous, but because she had paid attention. Another student preferred a hostel where guests shared a kitchen and could exchange practical advice. She had made a reservation for the first night, yet left the following morning open. When rain blocked the footpath, the group had to adapt rather than force the original plan. A covered market gave them shelter, a warm drink, and time to compare their expectations. Their conversation shifted perspective: unfamiliar places were not puzzles to conquer but communities to meet. The seminar did not suggest that planning or safety checks were unnecessary. It recommended a flexible itinerary, reliable contacts, and enough time to reflect after an unexpected change. Students wrote one question about what they hoped to learn before choosing a destination. Later, they described how each detour could transform their attention to ordinary life at home. Their conclusion was simple: a meaningful journey is measured by what you notice and reconsider.

section_b.title: Traveling Solo: Room to Adapt
section_b.passage: Mei had traveled with family before, but her first solo departure made a familiar station feel enormous. She checked her reservation twice, placed a small card with the hostel address in her pocket, and told her sister when she expected to arrive. Packing light luggage let her keep one hand free for her ticket and phone. She had expected confidence to arrive before the trip began, but it came in smaller decisions. At the platform, she felt nervous and reminded herself why she had chosen to go. Her itinerary named the hostel and one museum, while leaving the afternoon unplanned. After checking in, she asked the desk clerk which streets remained busy before dusk. The clerk marked a simple route to a market and advised her to avoid a closed riverside path. Mei used the map to navigate the first turns, then put it away to notice shop signs and sounds. When she missed a turning, she did not pretend to understand the route. A local bookseller showed her a safer street and asked what she hoped to see. That encounter became a memorable conversation about the neighborhood's changing shops. Mei began to wander slowly, choosing a public square rather than chasing a distant destination. A sudden rain shower made the shortest path slippery, so she adapted and waited under a covered stall. The landscape looked different from beneath the awning, and a shop owner offered tea while the rain passed. By returning to the hostel before dusk, Mei kept her trip both open and sensible. Her journal noted that independence does not require refusing help. She had once thought a fixed itinerary was the only protection from uncertainty. Now she would rather ask a respectful question than follow a confusing route alone. The journey transformed her perspective: solo travel could combine preparation, curiosity, and trust.

section_c.title: Stories of China
section_c.passage: In an original practice story, Lin leaves Chengdu for Xi'an on a high-speed train to meet her cousin. She has visited stations with classmates, but never studied a route as part of a reading assignment. Before departure, her teacher asks each traveler to note one expectation and one question. Lin expects a quick arrival and plans to photograph the station architecture. She carries light luggage, a notebook, and an itinerary with an afternoon left open. Across the aisle, a retired teacher is traveling to visit an old friend. They compare the route with the places each hopes to see, without claiming one person's plan is better. Their encounter begins with a question about the landscape beyond the window. The teacher describes how moving between cities has changed the work and family routines of people she knows. Lin listens, then adds the story to her notes rather than treating it as a universal rule. As the train continues, fields, rivers, and denser neighborhoods appear in sequence. The shifting landscape helps her notice that a route connects places without making them identical. She uses a map to follow the journey and ask how people navigate changes in daily life. A station announcement changes the arrival track, and passengers adapt calmly to new directions. Lin checks her destination, follows signs, and helps another traveler locate the correct platform. Later, her cousin shows her a street market that does not appear on the short itinerary. The local vendors explain how seasonal choices shape what they sell, and Lin asks permission before taking a photo. The trip's memorable moments come from conversations as much as scenery. On returning, Lin says travel can transform perspective when curiosity is joined to respect. Her class concludes that transport infrastructure offers a path, but people give the journey meaning.

listening.title: Listening: Let's go
listening.script: On my first solo journey, I thought successful travel meant following every point on an itinerary. I had made a reservation at a hostel and packed light luggage, so my departure felt organized. Yet a cancelled bus forced me to navigate a part of town I had not planned to see. I checked a printed route, asked a local shopkeeper for directions, and left enough time to wander safely. The detour led to a quiet garden and a memorable encounter with a woman who sold handmade paper. She explained how visitors often hurried past because they were trying to reach a famous destination before closing. Her comment changed my perspective. I began to notice the landscape, the shop signs, and the people whose routines continued around me. Later, rain made the path slippery, so I adapted and took a bus back to the hostel. I did not treat the change as a failure because I had built an alternative route into my plan. In my journal, I wrote that curiosity is not the same as ignoring safety. It means asking questions, checking directions, and staying open to a respectful conversation. Travel cannot promise that every encounter will transform us, but it can give us a reason to look more carefully. I would rather return with one new question than collect photos I never think about again.

section_a.title: What Makes Work Meaningful?
section_a.passage: At a campus career workshop, students gathered around a question that sounded simple but unsettled them: what makes work meaningful? The facilitator wrote worker and laborer on the board, then asked whether either word could measure a person's worth. One student associated laborer with strength and routine, while another imagined worker as someone who made decisions. The instructor warned that this attitude can quietly rank people before anyone understands what their jobs require. A task may be physical, repetitive, or performed behind the scenes, yet still demand close attention. The group visited a campus service team and watched a worker prepare a busy study room. She followed a routine checklist, but she also noticed a loose chair and stopped to report it. A student asked whether that extra judgment was part of the occupation or simply personal kindness. The worker explained that safety and dignity often depend on small decisions no checklist can predict. Later, a violin maker invited the class into a workshop. He asked his apprentice to compare two joints that looked almost identical. With careful precision, the apprentice measured the narrow gap that could alter the instrument's sound. The demonstration did not make one occupation more valuable than another; instead, it showed how knowledge and responsibility shape the quality of work. Back at the workshop, the students revised their first definitions and saw that skill can grow inside a routine and that craft is not limited to objects displayed in galleries. The instructor asked everyone to name one contribution they had previously overlooked. Students mentioned cleaners, repairers, cooks, and laboratory assistants. Each example required different knowledge, but each could protect another person's time, safety, or trust. The discussion ended without ranking the jobs, and the students agreed that meaningful work is not defined by a title alone. Pride becomes durable when people take responsibility for quality and treat those affected by their work with respect. That kind of fulfillment can belong to many occupations.

section_b.title: A Craft Tradition, Practiced with Care
section_b.passage: When Lin first entered the violin workshop, the master gave the apprentice a repair that seemed almost finished. A narrow joint still needed attention, although it was difficult to see without a lamp, so the master asked Lin to measure it twice and explain what the numbers meant. Lin wanted to hurry because a customer was waiting, but the master reminded him that a beautiful surface could hide a weak connection. A gap that was too wide might change the instrument's sound and shorten the repair's life. Lin repeated the measurement, adjusted the piece, and tested the fit before using glue. The routine felt slow, yet each step answered a different question about strength and balance. The master explained that precision was not perfection for its own sake; it was a promise about how the instrument would perform. Months later, Lin began to teach the same routine to a new apprentice. He kept the useful checks but also tried a digital gauge beside the workshop's older tool. Rather than accepting novelty or rejecting it, he compared the readings and asked whether the new method made the result clearer. When it did, he recorded the procedure so the whole team could use it. His dedication grew through repeated practice, and his passion became visible in how carefully he explained mistakes. A customer returned after hearing the repaired violin in a small concert. She thanked Lin not only for restoring the sound but also for describing what had been changed. That honest conversation strengthened trust between the workshop and its neighbors. Lin understood that tradition was not a command to repeat every motion forever. It was a body of knowledge carried forward, examined, and improved when evidence justified a change. The craft would remain rewarding only if young workers could learn, question, and contribute. In the final lesson of the day, the master asked Lin to name the standard he hoped to pass on. Lin answered: protect the work, respect the person who depends on it, and pursue excellence without confusing speed with skill.

section_c.title: Stories of China
section_c.passage: In this original learning story, a student named Mei visits a small silk-embroidery workshop in Suzhou with her class. She expects to see finished patterns, but the guide introduces the artisans who prepare the threads and study the designs, and Mei notices that a flower is not copied by counting colors alone. Each maker considers how a line turns, where the fabric will be used, and which details must remain clear. An artisan invites the students to look closely at a sample under a lamp. Mei records the explanation and asks before taking a photograph. The group learns that respect begins by listening to the people who hold the knowledge. At the next table, an apprentice practices a short row of stitches. Her mentor corrects the angle gently and asks her to describe what changed. The repeated exercise is not empty routine; it trains the hand to control tension and the eye to notice uneven thread. The student sees that heritage is carried by people who work, teach, and make decisions today. Later, the team discusses a new design for a community exhibition. They keep a familiar motif but adjust its size so visitors can see the stitch pattern from a distance. The change is reviewed with the makers rather than imposed by the visitors. Mei asks how the workshop can make this labor sustainable. The guide explains that fair payment, credit for makers, and opportunities to teach matter as much as displaying beautiful objects. Before leaving, each student chooses one question to investigate instead of claiming to understand the whole craft in an afternoon. Mei writes that an occupation can create income and also protect a shared memory. Her class understands that dignity is not supplied by praise alone; it grows when skilled people can make choices and be recognized for them. The visit changes their idea of tradition: it is not a silent object behind glass, but living knowledge practiced with care, renewed with permission, and shared across generations. These stories of China show how meaningful work can connect personal skill, community identity, and a future that still has room to change.

reading.title: More Than a Paycheck
reading.passage: A neighborhood repair cooperative was preparing for its annual open workshop. Its members included a bicycle mechanic, a seamstress, a cook, and a retired engineer. At first, visitors asked which occupation was the most skilled. The coordinator changed the question: what evidence would show that a job had been done well? The mechanic pointed to a safe brake test, while the seamstress showed how a repaired seam could bear weight without tearing. The cook described how timing and temperature protected both flavor and food safety. The engineer explained that a clear instruction sheet could prevent a costly mistake for the next person. None of these examples depended on a prestigious title. Each required knowledge, practice, and responsibility for someone who would use the result. During the workshop, a teenager helped repair a lamp. She wanted to replace a loose part quickly, but the engineer asked her to test why it had loosened. They found a worn screw and chose a stronger fitting. The teenager wrote down the steps so another volunteer could repeat the repair safely. Later, she told the group that the task felt rewarding because she understood its purpose and could see who benefited. The coordinator added that good work also needs fair conditions: reasonable time, safe tools, honest credit, and a chance to learn. The cooperative did not claim that every job was enjoyable every day. Instead, its members showed how pride can grow when a person is trusted, supported, and able to improve a result. By closing time, visitors had repaired several items and learned to ask better questions about labor. Quality was visible in the object, but meaning came from the care, judgment, and shared responsibility behind it.

listening.title: Listening: When work is a pleasure
listening.script: Welcome to the community workshop. Today we are looking at a repaired wooden chair, but the lesson is not simply about furniture. First, ask what the chair must do: support a person safely, remain stable, and last through ordinary use. The repairer checked each joint before adding a new piece of wood. She explained that a quick repair might look finished while leaving the chair weak underneath. A volunteer suggested copying the old method exactly. The repairer agreed that the older method contained useful knowledge, then showed how a new clamp made the pressure easier to control. The team tested the clamp on a sample before changing its routine. That small experiment helped them keep the sound principle and improve one step. A student asked whether this kind of work could be called creative. The repairer answered that creativity is not limited to painting or performance. It can also mean noticing a problem, selecting a method, and taking responsibility for the result. She invited the student to explain each choice aloud. When the student missed a safety check, the repairer gave immediate feedback and asked her to try again. The second attempt was slower but more accurate. At the end, the chair was tested under weight and the repair was recorded for the next volunteer. The team did not celebrate speed alone. They discussed who would use the chair, what evidence showed the repair was safe, and what they should review next week. A useful tradition, the repairer said, is knowledge that remains open to careful testing. Work becomes more satisfying when people can practice, receive feedback, and see the value their effort brings to others. Thank you for listening; after the questions, choose one example and explain the evidence that supports your answer.

section_a.question: Why did the far-side probe need a relay link to communicate with Earth?

section_a.question: What is the main purpose of repeating tests before a landing?

section_a.explanation: The passage treats tests as evidence about performance under specified conditions, not as proof that a system can never fail.

section_a.question: What helped the two student groups resolve their disagreement about the landing site?

section_a.question: What does Lin learn about exploration by the end of the passage?
options: A successful mission depends mainly on one brilliant inventor.

A dream becomes more reliable when generations inherit methods for testing it.
Future teams should repeat every earlier decision without review.

section_b.question: Why did the simulation team add a relay satellite to its model?

It could carry a message around the Moon's obstruction.
It allowed the spacecraft to skip orbit planning.
section_b.explanation: The direct radio route is blocked in the simulation, so the relay creates a communication path.

section_b.question: Why did An compare several sensor readings before changing the orbit?
options: To separate a confirmed drift from an uncertain reading before acting.
To prove that the spacecraft should never be adjusted.
To reduce the number of people involved in the mission.
To make the control-room display more impressive.
section_b.explanation: The team labels confirmed, estimated, and uncertain information so that a decision rests on reliable evidence.

section_b.question: What did the follow-up trial show about the smaller correction?
options: It restored the signal only by ignoring the fuel limit.
It made the relay unnecessary for later communication.
It worked in every possible condition without further testing.
It restored the signal with less fuel under the tested conditions.
section_b.explanation: The trial supports the smaller change for the tested setup; it does not establish that it works under every condition.

section_b.question: Why did An record both the successful result and its limitation?
options: To hide the uncertain readings from the next team.
So another team can understand what was tested and where caution is still needed.
To show that a breakthrough never requires revision.
So the mission can be judged by speed alone.
section_b.explanation: Recording the result and its boundary makes the procedure reviewable and prevents one test from being overstated.

section_c.question: What does Rui discover about astronaut preparation?
options: A strong launch vehicle is enough to prepare a crew.
Training is mainly a public performance before launch.
An astronaut can rely on instinct instead of practicing procedures.
Technical knowledge, physical readiness, judgment, and team practice work together.
section_c.explanation: The exhibit connects systems knowledge, physical and psychological preparation, emergency procedures, and coordination.

section_c.question: What does the simulated warning teach the trainee to do first?
options: Silence the alarm and continue the planned task.
Wait for one teammate to make every decision.
Follow a checklist, communicate the reading, and confirm the next safe step.
Change the spacecraft setting before checking the data.
section_c.explanation: The scenario rewards a deliberate sequence: use the procedure, share evidence, and confirm a safe response.

section_c.question: Why does the exhibit include a model of a space station as well as a rocket?
options: Long-term work in orbit depends on systems and research after launch, too.
A station removes the effects of gravity from every experiment.
A station is used only to display a launch vehicle.
The exhibit wants visitors to ignore crew preparation.
section_c.explanation: The station model helps Rui see that sustained experiments, maintenance, and crew routines continue after a launch.

section_c.question: Which idea best summarizes the passage's view of a space frontier?
options: Only astronauts contribute to a space program.
A frontier is meaningful when careful preparation and shared research let people explore responsibly.
Scientific success should be measured by publicity rather than evidence.
Training can stop once the first mission has succeeded.
section_c.explanation: The ending links exploration with disciplined preparation, reliable systems, and work shared across generations.

section_a.title: No limit for China's astronauts in their space exploration endeavors
section_a.passage: At a university mission exhibit, Lin received a blank map of the Moon and a question: why does the far side ask more of a spacecraft than a powerful engine can provide? He drew Earth behind the lunar disk, then placed a relay satellite where both Earth and the hidden landing area could be reached. Only then did the communication problem become visible: a probe behind the Moon cannot send a direct radio signal to a ground station. The exhibit explained that Chang'e-4 achieved the first soft landing and rover operations on the lunar far side in 2019, supported by the Queqiao relay link. Lin had celebrated the breakthrough as a single moment, but the guide asked him to see the mission as a chain of decisions. A launch window, a planned orbit, and a controlled landing each depend on different checks. Before a model spacecraft descended, the team rehearsed the sequence in simulation and agreed on what every sensor should report. When one reading falls outside its expected range, engineers compare it with other data before changing course. The purpose of a test is not to prove a design perfect but to learn whether it works under specified conditions. Lin wrote down the claim, the evidence, and the uncertainty instead of trusting the brightest image. At the display, an animation showed the relay passing a message between the far-side probe and Earth. Lin followed the signal route with his finger and saw how cooperation joined operators, scientists, and equipment across distance. Research and innovation therefore appeared not as slogans but as tools for solving a communication constraint. A telescope can reveal a distant surface, yet a landing still requires measurements, communication, and safe decisions close to the Moon. The guide called the scientific frontier a place where curiosity must become a testable question. Students next received sample data and had to decide which model site was level enough for a safe descent. Two groups disagreed because they had used different reference points on the same slope. When they compared their methods, they found that one sensor had been read from the wrong scale. Lin revised his answer and explained why the corrected evidence changed the landing choice. He left with a more ambitious idea of exploration: each generation inherits not only a dream, but a method for checking it.

section_b.title: Chang'e-4 kicked off a new space odyssey
section_b.passage: In a campus control-room simulation, An joined a team asked to deliver a message from a lunar probe hidden behind the Moon. A direct route disappeared from the screen whenever the Moon blocked the line between the probe and Earth. Their model added a relay satellite, turning one broken connection into two monitored links. An wanted to move the spacecraft immediately, but the mentor asked her to inspect the data log first. The orbit trace showed a small drift; a second sensor confirmed it, while a third reading remained uncertain. The team labeled each fact, estimate, and open question rather than treating every number as equally reliable. They checked how a correction would affect fuel, timing, and the next communication window. No single control carried the whole mission: navigation, communication, and science teams had to compare their evidence. When An simulated an orbit adjustment, the relay link returned, but the margin for error narrowed. She recorded both the successful result and the condition that could make it fail. The mentor explained that a breakthrough is repeatable only when its method is documented and tested. The class then compared two designs, one simpler and one more ambitious. Students chose neither because it looked advanced; they asked what test would distinguish them. A follow-up trial showed that the smaller change restored the signal with less fuel under the tested conditions. This choice was not a rejection of innovation but a decision guided by evidence. An understood why exploration requires both courage and restraint. A lunar odyssey stretches across years, yet each careful check protects the next step. The simulation ended with an unanswered question about communication reliability. Rather than guess, the team planned a new trial and assigned one task to each member. An left the control room seeing cooperation not as a slogan, but as a way to expose weak assumptions before they became costly.

section_c.title: Stories of China
section_c.passage: At a science center, Rui expected an astronaut exhibit to focus on rockets, but the first room showed a crew practicing ordinary procedures. A guide explained that astronaut candidates study spacecraft systems and rehearse physical, psychological, and emergency tasks before a mission. Their preparation is an endeavor measured in careful practice, not a dramatic countdown. In a training pool, a crew learns to move steadily while a partner checks the route and the equipment. A simulated warning then interrupts the exercise. The trainee reads the panel, reports the data, and waits for the team to confirm which procedure applies. One student asks why the crew does not simply react by instinct. The guide answers that in a complex environment, practiced communication can prevent a small uncertainty from becoming a larger risk. The next display shows how gravity affects movement and why a station needs routines for work, rest, and research. A telescope is not just an impressive object on the wall; it represents questions that scientists can investigate when instruments, people, and records work together. Rui sees that a spacecraft launch is only one stage in a longer system. After liftoff, teams monitor the orbit, support the crew, and interpret results. The exhibit asks visitors to match each mission task with the evidence that would show it was completed safely. Rui first chooses a photograph, then notices that a checklist, measurement, and crew report provide stronger support. The group discusses how cooperation connects engineers on Earth with astronauts in orbit. Their work opens a frontier, but it also depends on shared preparation and public investment in research. Before leaving, Rui writes one question for a future science lesson and one skill he could practice now: explain a claim with evidence. He understands that exploration is not a promise of easy answers. It is a disciplined way for people across generations to ask better questions and test them together.

reading.title: The Message That Crossed the Moon
reading.passage: During a public science workshop, a student team had to design a communication plan for a probe on the Moon's far side. Their first sketch pointed a radio line straight toward Earth, but a lunar model blocked it. A mentor asked the students to identify the constraint before adding equipment. They placed a relay satellite where it could pass messages between the hidden probe and Earth, then drew a second route for backup communication. The model did not prove that a real mission would succeed; it helped the team ask which parts would need testing. They listed power, orbit, timing, and signal quality as separate questions. One group wanted to choose a path because it looked shortest. Another compared the angles and found that a slightly longer route offered a clearer link. The students recorded what their model showed and what it could not show. Their report distinguished evidence from assumption and suggested a next test rather than claiming certainty. The mentor connected the exercise with Chang'e-4, whose far-side operations depended on a relay link because the Moon interrupts direct communication. The historic result was not a shortcut around engineering; it was evidence that careful system design can make a difficult task possible. By the end, the students understood that exploration is a chain: a question guides a model, a test challenges the model, and new data shapes the next decision. A successful mission may make headlines, but the habits that support it are patient research, clear records, and cooperation across different specialties.

questions.question: What problem did the lunar model reveal in the team's first sketch?

questions.question: What does the report distinguish?

Public interest from scientific research.
The relay satellite from the spacecraft.
The Moon's near side from its craters.
questions.explanation: The students record what their model demonstrates, what it cannot show, and what should be tested next.

questions.explanation: The passage closes with a chain from question to model, test, evidence, and collaboration.

listening.title: Listening: A Test Before the Next Step
listening.script: Welcome to the mission-training room. Today, our crew is not launching a spacecraft; it is rehearsing what to do when a sensor gives an unexpected reading. First, the trainee reads the procedure and says the value aloud. A teammate checks the number against a second display, while the instructor records the time and the system's status. The team does not change the orbit just because one signal looks unusual. They compare the data, identify what remains uncertain, and decide whether the mission rule calls for a pause or a correction. In a separate exercise, the crew practices moving through a station module in low gravity. The goal is not speed. Each person must secure the equipment, report a change, and leave a clear note for the next shift. After the rehearsal, the group reviews one mistake without blaming the trainee. They ask which cue was missed and how the checklist can make the next attempt safer. The instructor says that research missions depend on accurate instruments, but also on people who communicate honestly. When a later test improves the procedure, the change is recorded and shared with the whole team. A space mission may be ambitious, yet its reliability is built from small actions that can be checked and repeated. For your question, listen for the evidence the crew uses before it acts.

questions.question: What does the crew do before changing the orbit in response to an unusual signal?
options: They silence the alarm and continue without recording it.
They ask one specialist to decide without checking the procedure.
They compare the reading with other data and identify uncertainty.
They change the spacecraft setting immediately.
questions.explanation: The team checks a second display and identifies uncertainty before deciding whether to pause or correct.

questions.question: What is the goal of the low-gravity station exercise?

To avoid communicating with the next shift.

questions.explanation: The exercise emphasizes safe equipment handling, clear reporting, and handover rather than speed.

questions.question: How does the instructor respond to a mistake in rehearsal?
options: The instructor removes the trainee from the next exercise.
The team identifies the missed cue and improves the checklist without blame.
The mistake is hidden so that the schedule stays on time.
The crew stops documenting procedures.
questions.explanation: The group asks what cue was missed and how the checklist can improve, without blaming the trainee.

questions.question: Which idea best captures the speaker's final point?
options: A mission is reliable when its small actions can be checked and repeated.
Only advanced equipment matters in scientific work.
A procedure should never change after its first use.
An ambitious mission can succeed without honest communication.
questions.explanation: The closing lines connect reliability with repeatable, checkable actions and honest communication.

units.title: The economy: power behind everyday life
units.title_zh: 经济：日常生活背后的力量

section_a.question: Which pressures first put Lantern Books at risk?
options: A sudden surplus of books and lower delivery costs
A plan to move the store to a larger building
Rising rent and delivery costs during a recession, alongside a tight budget
A new rule requiring every reader to buy a book
section_a.explanation: The opening links the recession and inflation to higher rent and delivery costs, while the budget and savings are shrinking.

section_a.question: What did Mei and the campus club build to respond to readers' needs?
options: A larger shop stocked only brand-new titles.
A book-sharing wall, funded by a small loan and run as a measured pilot.
A delivery service that charged readers before showing the books.
A private club that stopped serving neighborhood consumers.
section_a.explanation: Mei used a small loan to build weatherproof shelves, then the club tracked exchanges during a two-week pilot.

section_a.question: Why did the exchange not automatically mean higher profit or effortless service?
options: Cleaning, sorting, and checking missing copies still took staff time.

The shop stopped keeping any records of its inventory.

section_a.question: What best explains the bookstore's modest resilience by the end of term?
options: A single investment guaranteed a large profit.
The neighborhood no longer needed affordable reading.
The shop stopped listening to customers and club members.
Trust, clear records, cooperation, and repeated adjustments kept value circulating.
section_a.explanation: The ending credits resilience to trust, records, repair, and adjustment, not a guaranteed windfall.

section_b.question: What was the campus club's first goal for its book exchange?
options: To promise instant revenue to every member
To replace the campus library with a commercial store
To make useful books affordable and keep them circulating among readers
To collect damaged books without recording their condition
section_b.explanation: The opening frames the project as access and reuse, not as a promise of immediate profit.

section_b.question: Which practice helped users trust the exchange during its pilot?
options: Logging book condition, exchanges, and clear return responsibilities
Keeping the fee and the checkout rules secret
Letting the first user decide who could borrow next
Removing all records to make the process faster
section_b.explanation: Transparent condition notes and checkout records make responsibility visible and disputes easier to resolve.

section_b.question: Why did the club compare staffing and repair costs before expanding?
options: They planned to stop recording damage and returns.
They wanted to prove that any increase in loans guarantees fair access.
A sponsor had already promised to cover every future cost.
A new site could add reach but weaken local support if no partner maintained the books.
section_b.explanation: The passage names staffing and repair costs, then warns that expansion could weaken local support without a maintenance partner.

section_b.question: Which test best shows whether the project can continue responsibly?
options: Count only the most popular books on opening day.
Compare access, maintenance costs, local-shop support, and user feedback over time.
Measure success only by how quickly the project expands.
Assume that every sharing platform is fair by definition.
section_b.explanation: The final scene treats sustainability as a balance of usefulness, affordability, costs, and feedback.

section_c.question: In the students' fictional county case, what first made reading harder for families?
options: A sudden increase in free transport to the library

A rule that families could use only printed maps

section_c.question: Why did the library keep an assisted, offline option alongside digital lending?
options: Some residents lacked reliable devices or felt unsure using the platform.

The library wanted to prevent volunteers from helping readers.

section_c.explanation: The story identifies device access and confidence as barriers, so a human-assisted route remains important.

section_c.question: How did cooperation improve the service rather than merely add publicity?
options: Partners removed every lending rule and condition check.
The library transferred all decisions to one sponsor.
Residents stopped reporting problems with access.
Readers, volunteers, and librarians found barriers and adjusted the service together.
section_c.explanation: The partners used reader feedback to improve assistance, catalog guidance, and device access.

section_c.question: What would be the strongest evidence that the library project is resilient?
options: A large download count, even if many users cannot open the books
A one-time donation with no plan for maintenance
Sustained reading access, manageable costs, and useful feedback from different residents
An announcement that the service will never need revision
section_c.explanation: Resilience is shown by lasting access and an ability to learn and adapt, not by a single headline number.

section_a.title: Surviving an economic crisis
section_a.passage: In the old harbor district, Lantern Books had served students for twenty years, but a recession changed the street. Inflation pushed up rent and delivery costs, while a tight budget left fewer new titles on its shelves. Owner Mei wrote each expense beside the supply of books and the demand from readers instead of guessing. Her savings covered only two months, and she feared the shop would close before the next school term. To understand the crisis, she asked customers what they needed and what they could afford. A campus club suggested a sharing wall where a reader could leave one book and choose another. Mei took a small loan to build weatherproof shelves and a simple checkout desk. During a two-week pilot, every exchange was entered in a paper ledger with a fair, affordable fee. The club recorded the book condition, the reader's choice, and the time each title remained on the shelf. The early numbers showed that a few popular subjects moved quickly while other titles waited. Rather than call the project an instant success, Mei compared its modest revenue with saved purchasing costs. Reusing books improved efficiency, but cleaning, sorting, and missing-copy checks still required staff time. Some consumers could not pay even a small fee, so the club created a no-fee exchange hour. The change widened access without hiding the real cost of keeping the service open. Mei explained that sharing works only when rules protect both the resource and the people using it. By the end of the term, the shop had not become rich, yet it had kept two local jobs and reopened a quiet reading corner. Readers returned with suggestions, and the club helped repair damaged covers instead of discarding every copy. This modest resilience came from trust, clear records, and repeated adjustments rather than one heroic investment. Students traced how price, supply, demand, and access shaped ordinary choices in the neighborhood. They left with a practical lesson: a healthy economy depends on choices that keep value circulating and responsibility visible.

section_b.title: The sharing economy turns a new page with books
section_b.passage: On campus, a club found that students often bought a required book for one term and then let it collect dust. They designed a sharing exchange where members could lend or swap a copy through a staffed locker. The organizers called it Page Loop, an original student startup built to expand access, not promise instant revenue. Before opening, they surveyed consumers about prices, titles, and whether a refundable deposit felt fair. Their first design offered one flat fee, but readers warned that the rule could exclude people with a tight budget. The team revised the model: a small affordable charge covered checks, while members could volunteer during free-access hours. A barcode, condition note, and clear return date let volunteers track supply without treating every user as a risk. During a month-long trial, they logged which titles moved, which stayed untouched, and when the line grew. Demand shifted around exam weeks, so the club added high-use titles and asked departments to donate older editions. The records also revealed a bottleneck: volunteers spent too long checking books at a single desk. They arranged two return boxes and a short inspection rota, improving efficiency without removing a human check. One sponsor suggested rapid expansion, but the club compared extra staffing and repair costs first. The new site would add reach, yet could weaken local support if no partner helped maintain the books. A teacher asked the group to distinguish activity from impact: more loans did not automatically mean fairer access. Members compared user feedback, wait times, damaged copies, and costs before changing the rules. They kept a free weekly hour for students who could not pay, supported by a campus fund. During that hour, exchange still followed the same condition and return standards. After one term, the project had modest revenue and stronger ties between the club and the campus shop. The team described the model as sustainable only if access, maintenance, and local cooperation remained in balance. Page Loop taught them that sharing works best when transparency makes responsibility as visible as convenience.

section_c.title: Stories of China: A Fictional County Library Case
section_c.passage: For a class project, students created a fictional county case called Yunhe to examine access to reading during a downturn. In their story, many families had a tight budget, and the county library could not buy every new title. The students proposed a shared digital-lending catalog so one licensed copy could reach more readers over time. They did not present Yunhe as a documented real event; it was a model for testing choices, costs, and access. Their first question was simple: who might still be left out if the service moved online? A group of older residents had no reliable device, while some families shared one phone among several people. Librarians therefore kept printed guides and an assisted desk beside the digital screen. Volunteers helped readers request a title, set a return reminder, and find an offline alternative when needed. The team listed the resources: licenses, devices, staff time, network access, and community knowledge. Demand rose before exams, so a booking queue showed where extra copies or longer lending periods mattered. The students compared costs with the number of completed reads rather than counting clicks alone. A local school offered quiet study space, and a community group helped troubleshoot basic device problems. These partners could not erase the recession, but they reduced barriers that price alone could not explain. The library also collected feedback in short interviews, including from people who had not used the service. Their comments led to clearer instructions, larger text, and a weekly in-person help session. One student argued that digital lending was always more efficient, but the access notes challenged that claim. A shared platform saved travel for some readers while still requiring licenses, maintenance, and human support. In the fictional case, resilience meant keeping useful knowledge accessible while adjusting the system as needs changed. The class concluded that communities invest in one another when they plan for both convenience and exclusion. Their final report asked readers to judge an economy by who can participate, what it costs, and whether the value lasts.

reading.title: The Library of Useful Things
reading.passage: When a student housing cooperative noticed that residents were buying tools they used only once, it proposed a small lending room. At first, the idea sounded simple: place a drill, a sewing kit, and a bicycle pump on a shelf, then let anyone borrow them. But the student team quickly learned that access depends on more than putting objects in a room. A tool needs an inspection record, a return date, and a person responsible for checking damage. The cooperative created a modest membership fee to cover repairs, while reserving free borrowing hours for residents facing a tight budget. Its first month produced an unexpected pattern. The bicycle pump moved every week, but the drill waited until a repair workshop advertised its availability. Demand was therefore not a fixed number; it changed with information and timing. One resident argued that the team should buy more equipment immediately. Another asked them to compare actual use with storage and maintenance costs before spending the cooperative's limited saving. They checked the log, asked neighbors what repairs they planned, and borrowed a second drill from a nearby community center for one weekend. This test met the short-term need without creating an unnecessary purchase. The project also exposed a fairness problem: residents who worked late could not reach the room before it closed. Volunteers added a staffed evening slot and a simple booking board. The system did not remove every cost, and it was not automatically sustainable just because people shared. It became more useful when clear rules protected the tools, transparent records showed what was needed, and residents could suggest changes. By the end of the term, the cooperative had a better estimate of which resources deserved investment. The lesson was practical: a sharing economy is a set of choices about access, responsibility, and value, not merely a shelf of free things.

listening.title: Listening: Should the campus expand its book exchange?
listening.script: Welcome back to the campus economics podcast. Our student group has run a book exchange for one term, and the first result is encouraging but incomplete. More than a hundred books changed hands, yet the number alone cannot tell us whether the project was fair or sustainable. We compared the titles requested, the waiting time, repair costs, and the comments from students who could not pay the regular fee. During exam weeks, demand rose for a few subjects, so the club borrowed extra copies from two departments instead of purchasing a large stock. We also kept a free-access hour supported by a small campus fund. That choice widened access, but volunteers still had to inspect returns and maintain the shelves. A local shop now offers a discount on basic repairs, which keeps some spending in the community. Before expanding to another building, the club will run a second trial and ask evening students about opening hours. In other words, we will not treat popularity as proof of success. The more carefully we track costs and listen to users, the more responsibly we can decide what to share. A strong local economy is not simply about moving more goods; it is about making useful exchange possible while keeping its rules, costs, and benefits visible.
